headline: A really good business can produce disappointing returns if priced for perfection; a mediocre company can generate excellent returns if expectations were excessively pessimistic
reasoning: Investing is not a simple mathematical formula where good fundamentals mechanically produce good returns. What matters is how a company's earnings and fundamentals compare to the collective expectations already embedded in the share price. A high-quality company whose strong performance is already anticipated will see a stagnant or disappointing share price — as illustrated by employees who receive company shares and cannot understand why strong earnings produce no price gain. Conversely, a mediocre business can outperform if market expectations were excessively negative. This is the game-theory dimension of investing: outcomes depend not just on fundamentals but on the decisions and perceptions of all other market participants.
quote: And we're not saying that company earnings and other fundamentals don't matter. They of course do. But, it also matters how they compare to everyone else's expectations. And that really matters in terms of the outcome that you will achieve. So, really good business can produce disappointing investment returns if it's priced for perfection. On the other hand, a mediocre company can generate excellent returns if those expectations were excessively pessimistic.
episode_title: Why Smart Investors Still Lose Money

headline: Extreme pessimism in April 2025 tariff turmoil drove herd selling via loss aversion, while extreme optimism fuels bubble-buying — both are prisoner's-dilemma dynamics that destroy investor returns
reasoning: During the April 2025 tariff turmoil, investor sentiment surveys and the put/call ratio showed extreme pessimism, leading investors to sell en masse to avoid being 'left holding the bag.' This is driven by loss aversion — losses feel twice as painful as equivalent gains — causing selling that begets more selling. The mirror dynamic occurs in bubbles, where investors buy not because prices are justified but because they expect someone else to pay even more tomorrow. The key insight is that this behaviour doesn't require irrationality; it simply requires investors responding to their perception of the incentives they face. The optimal path — analogous to both prisoners staying silent — is for investors to remain patient during corrections, focus on fundamentals, and avoid portfolio decisions based on anticipating what everyone else will do.
quote: And what we see in the graph is extreme pessimism that often leads to large dips in the index where investors clamor to remove themselves before others do. They don't want to be the ones that are left holding the bag. And this is an example of the concept of loss aversion where a loss feels twice as painful as an equivalent gain. And then on the other side of that, of course, is when there's extreme optimism and that is when investors are trying to get into the market to capitalize on gains that they foresee before others do that. Now, imagine a world where more investors remain patient during a market correction. Share prices would likely recover much quicker and everyone would benefit. But instead, what we actually see in real life is that many investors sell because they fear others are going to sell and they're trying to get out of the market first.
episode_title: Why Smart Investors Still Lose Money
